targetKeywords: how to teach children to question claims
title: Why Critical Thinking Matters for Children
metaDescription: How to help children tell evidence from confidence, spot persuasive claims, and reason through everyday decisions, including ones about money.

sections.heading: Why this is a money skill, not just a classroom skill
paragraphs: Children meet persuasive claims constantly - an advert, a friend's confident opinion, a game promising a reward, a message that something is scarce or urgent. Critical thinking is simply the habit of pausing on a claim before accepting or acting on it: who's making it, what evidence backs it up, and what it wants the listener to do next. Money is one of the clearest places to practise this, because so many claims a child encounters - 'this is a bargain', 'everyone has one', 'you'll miss out' - are specifically designed to bypass that pause.

This article is about the general habit of evaluating claims and evidence, with money as one recurring example among several. It's a close relative of, but distinct from, learning to sort needs from wants: that's a specific category judgement about a single decision, while critical thinking is the broader skill of asking what's actually being claimed and how you'd check it, which applies just as much to a friend's opinion or a game's promised reward as it does to a purchase.

sections.heading: Start with claims children already encounter
paragraphs: You don't need an abstract lesson in logic to begin - children can recognise persuasive language well before they could define it. A simple way in: show a fictional poster claiming 'Everyone needs this toy!' and ask three plain questions. Who made this claim? What evidence do they give for it? What do they want me to do next? Most children, even quite young ones, can answer all three once they've been asked a couple of times, because the pattern - someone wants me to do something, and is using a strong claim to get there - is one they half-notice already.

sections.heading: Model changing your mind out loud
paragraphs: One of the most useful things an adult can do is narrate their own reasoning when it changes, rather than only modelling confident, finished conclusions. Try saying something like: 'I thought this was the cheaper one, but I forgot to add the delivery cost - let me compare the total price instead.' This is a UK-style phrasing using pounds as the example currency; the same idea works with any currency, just swap the units. The point isn't the specific numbers - it's showing a child that revising a decision when new information turns up is what good thinking looks like, not a failure to have got it right the first time.

sections.heading: A three-question routine you can use anywhere
paragraphs: A short, repeatable routine travels better than a one-off lesson. Three questions cover most everyday claims: What is the claim, exactly? How could we check it? What else might explain it? Use them on familiar, low-stakes material - a price, an online recommendation, a claim about a game's rewards - rather than saving them for big decisions, so the habit is already comfortable by the time it matters. One caution worth building in from the start: use the routine as a genuine question, not as the opening move of a debate. A child who feels cross-examined every time they say something stops volunteering claims to test at all, which defeats the purpose.

sections.heading: Teach productive uncertainty, not blanket doubt
paragraphs: Some questions have a clean, checkable answer. Whether £4 plus £3 fits inside a £6 budget (a UK-style example in pounds; use your own currency's amounts if that's clearer for your child) is settled by arithmetic, not opinion. Other questions - which of two toys is more fun, whether a particular purchase is worth it - genuinely depend on priorities, and don't have one correct answer at all. Children benefit from learning to tell these apart, and from having permission to say 'I'm not sure yet' when a genuine answer requires information they don't currently have, rather than guessing confidently just to produce an answer.

sections.heading: A worked example across three ages
paragraphs: Here's one scenario, scaled for different ages. A fictional advert claims a £12 product (a UK-style example in pounds) is 'half price', but never states the original price it's half of.
list: Ages 6-8: ask simply, 'does the advert tell us what it used to cost?' If not, the child can learn that 'half price' isn't a fact yet - it's a claim missing a piece.
Ages 9-11: ask the child to compare this advert with a second one that does show both the original price and a delivery cost, and decide which offer actually gives them enough information to judge.
Ages 12-14: ask the child to propose what they'd need to see before trusting the 'half price' claim at all, and to explain what someone benefits from by leaving that information out.

sections.heading: A step-by-step way to run this with a group or a class
paragraphs: This structure works for a family conversation or a short classroom activity alike.
list: Present one simple, clearly fictional claim.
Ask what the claim actually says, and who benefits if people believe it.
Ask what information is missing, and one safe way it could be checked.
Invite a revised decision once the missing evidence is filled in, and ask the child to explain what changed their mind.

sections.heading: How to check whether a child actually understood
paragraphs: The test that matters isn't agreement - it's reasoning on a new example. Present a claim the child hasn't seen before and see whether they can, unprompted, identify what's missing or propose a fair way to compare two options. A child who respectfully disagrees with you and gives a sound reason for it is very often demonstrating stronger critical thinking than one who simply repeats back the adult's conclusion. If a child gives an answer you didn't expect, ask for their reasoning before correcting anything; sometimes it reveals a perfectly valid angle you hadn't considered, and sometimes it shows the instructions weren't fully understood - either way, the follow-up question teaches you more than the answer alone did.

sections.heading: Making this accessible for different learners
paragraphs: This kind of reasoning doesn't depend on fluent spoken language, and shouldn't be assessed as if it did. For a child with SEND (special educational needs and disabilities), break the three-question routine down to one question at a time rather than all three at once, use large, uncluttered images instead of a busy printed advert to reduce sensory load, and allow considerably more processing time before expecting a response. A child using AAC (augmentative and alternative communication) can take part fully with a small set of core symbols - 'true', 'not sure', 'missing', 'check' - covering most of what the three-question routine needs. Pointing to a symbol, selecting an option on a device, or physically sorting picture cards into 'checked' and 'not checked yet' piles are all valid, equally real demonstrations of the same reasoning a verbal child shows by explaining aloud.

sections.heading: A common mistake to avoid
paragraphs: It's tempting, once a child starts questioning claims well, to push the lesson further than it should go - treating every statement as equally uncertain, including ones that are genuinely checkable by simple arithmetic or direct observation. That's not critical thinking, it's just generalised doubt, and it can leave a child more confused rather than more capable. Keep the distinction explicit: some things can be settled with a calculation or a quick check, and the skill is knowing which kind of claim you're looking at, not assuming nothing can ever be known for sure.

sections.heading: Try this next
paragraphs: Pick one claim from something your child or class has actually seen this week - an advert, a game, a confident statement from a friend - and run the three-question routine on it together. Ask the child to explain their reasoning, show it with pictures, or communicate it in their preferred way, and keep any real family financial information out of the example; a fictional price or fictional scenario teaches exactly the same skill without requiring that kind of disclosure.

sections.heading: Editorial references
paragraphs: The emphasis throughout this article on getting children to explain and revise their own reasoning, rather than simply reach a correct answer, draws on the Education Endowment Foundation's summary of evidence on metacognition and self-regulation (educationendowmentfoundation.org.uk), which finds that pupils who are taught to plan, monitor and reflect on their own thinking tend to retain and transfer new learning more effectively. General guidance on age-appropriate financial education, including how children encounter persuasive claims around money specifically, draws on the Money and Pensions Service's work with children and young people (maps.org.uk).

faqs.question: How long should this kind of activity take?
faqs.answer: Ten to fifteen minutes is a reasonable starting point for most families or classrooms, but treat that as a practical suggestion rather than a fixed rule - adapt it to the child's attention span and any access needs, and it's fine to stop after one example if that's where genuine engagement ends.

faqs.question: Isn't teaching kids to question everything going to make them cynical?
faqs.answer: Not if the goal is clear: the aim is distinguishing checkable facts from unsupported claims, not treating everything as equally doubtful. A child who learns that some things genuinely can be verified, while others depend on evidence that's missing, ends up more confident in their own judgement, not more suspicious of everything.

faqs.question: What age can children start learning this?
faqs.answer: Even quite young children, around age 6-8, can answer simple versions of 'what does this claim say, and who made it?' The questions and expected depth of answer should scale up with age, but the underlying habit of pausing on a claim can start early.

faqs.question: What if my child gives an answer I didn't expect?
faqs.answer: Ask for their reasoning before correcting anything. An unexpected answer sometimes reveals a reasonable angle you hadn't considered, and sometimes shows the instructions weren't fully understood - either way, a follow-up question and another example usually clears it up.
